The session is 4 hours. The framework block is a recap of this page, which you read before class, so that most of the time goes to building. The build lab includes a 10-minute break.

::: {.callout-note title="How to use this page"}
- Read the topics in order. Each one opens with a guiding question and uses the Cerro Azul case.
- Every topic has at least one simulator. Predict what will happen before you touch it, then check.
- The "In the business" note says why the idea matters to a manager, not to a programmer.
- The practice questions explain why each wrong option is wrong. Retry as often as you like.
- The build lab is what your team does in class. Its prompts are meant to be copied and adapted, and the checklist is saved in your browser.
- Data rule: only invented or de-identified information until the session 4 lab is done, critical findings are closed and the data's owner has agreed in writing. No real names, phone numbers, addresses or tax numbers in the app, in the test set or in any prompt.
:::

## What you will be able to do

- Write a user story with acceptance criteria that an assistant can build without guessing.
- Work in small requests, test by using the app, save checkpoints, and roll back a bad change without reading code.
- Move QuoteDesk from a page that forgets everything to a managed database with a login for each rep.
- Specify four UX patterns for output that is sometimes wrong.
- Tell apart the three things people call "the AI": the assistant you build with, the assistant a rep works with, and the model inside the app.
- Write a project instructions file, and package "how we write a quote here" as a skill the assistant loads on its own.
- Connect your team's assistant to one company system through a connector, read-only, and say in one sentence what that door allows.
- Deliver milestone M2: the deployed prototype v1, with one skill and one connector.

## Topic 1 · Prompting as specification {#topic-1}

```{=html}
<p class="vc-guide"><strong>Guiding question:</strong> if the assistant builds exactly what you asked, why does it so often build the wrong thing?</p>
```

In session 1 your team wrote a brief and had a working page in under an hour. The second hour usually feels different: the assistant adds a button you never asked for, the list sorts the wrong way, "save" works on your laptop and not on your phone. None of that is the assistant being careless. It is the assistant filling the gaps you left with the most common answer from millions of other apps. A quote tool for a food distributor in Chile is not the most common app.

The fix is a habit, not a tool. Before you ask for a feature, write it as a **user story** with **acceptance criteria**. A user story is one sentence: *as a sales rep, I want to paste a customer message and save it as a quote request, so that I stop retyping it into the ERP.* Acceptance criteria are the three to six checks that tell you, and the assistant, when the story is done. With fewer than three you leave the decisions to the assistant. With more than six you have probably glued two stories together.

| Part | Weak | Strong |
|---|---|---|
| User | "users" | "a Cerro Azul sales rep on a phone, between customer visits" |
| Action | "handle quotes" | "paste a WhatsApp message and save it as a quote request for one named customer" |
| Done when | "it works" | "the request appears at the top of the list with date, rep and customer; empty messages are refused" |

Managers know this format from product teams. What is new is that the assistant reads it literally. Each criterion you write is one decision it does not have to guess. Each one you leave out is a surprise waiting in the next hour.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-spec"></div>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="In the business"}
Paula retyping a quote costs Cerro Azul about 12 minutes. A manager who specifies badly costs more: every vague request is a build, a test, a complaint and a rebuild. The assistant is cheap per attempt, but your team's two hours in the lab are not. Acceptance criteria are the cheapest insurance you will buy in this course.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="vc-practice">
<p class="vc-practice-t"><span>Practice · Topic 1</span></p>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Which of these is an acceptance criterion, as opposed to a wish?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="This is a goal. It says nothing a tester could check as done or not done.">The quote tool should be fast, clear and easy for reps to use on a phone between visits.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>An empty message cannot be saved; the save button stays disabled until there is text.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="This is the user story, the one-sentence framing. It still needs criteria to be testable.">As a rep, I want to save quote requests quickly so that I stop retyping them into the ERP.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">A criterion is a check that is either true or false when you use the app. "Cannot be saved when empty" is one. "Fast and easy" is a wish, and the assistant will decide for you what it means.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">The assistant added a "priority" dropdown to the quote request that nobody asked for. What most likely happened?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Assistants rarely refuse; they fill gaps. A missing instruction was the cause, not a technical limit.">The assistant could not build the fields you asked for, so it replaced them with something it could build.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>Your story did not list the fields of a quote request, so the assistant used the usual ones from similar apps.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="There is no hidden plan. The assistant produces the likeliest completion of your request, and 'priority' is common in ticket-style apps.">The assistant has its own plan for what the app should become and is quietly adding features toward that plan.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">Every unspecified field is a guess. Listing the fields (customer, message, date, rep, status) in the criteria removes the guess, and the dropdown.</p>
```

## Topic 2 · Small steps, checkpoints and undo {#topic-2}

```{=html}
<p class="vc-guide"><strong>Guiding question:</strong> how do you make it safe, and fast, to break the app?</p>
```

Every first-time builder repeats one pattern. Confidence is high, so the team pastes a single request: login, customer list, quote form, PDF export, email notification, dashboard. The assistant produces something that mostly runs. Then the login breaks the list, the PDF breaks the form, and nobody knows which of the six changes caused which of the four problems.

The alternative is boring and it works: **one story per request**. Ask for the customer picker. Use the app as Paula would, in a phone-sized window on your laptop (your browser can show any page at a phone's width). If it works, save a checkpoint. If it does not, you know what broke, because only one thing changed.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-steps"></div>
```

The rule has a second half: **test by using, not by reading**. You are not going to read the code and you do not need to. Do the rep's task end to end, including the cases that should fail. When something looks wrong, ask: *what did you change and why?* The answer is written in plain language, and it is often where you find the gap in your criteria.

Small steps are only cheap if going back is cheap. Software teams solve that with **version control** (the usual tool is Git, with the history kept online on GitHub). You will use it through the assistant, so you need three ideas, not the commands:

- A **checkpoint** (a commit) is a named snapshot of the whole app at a moment it worked. In this course, saving a checkpoint always includes sending it to GitHub, which is what updates your public address a minute later. "Customer picker working" is a good name. Save one after every story that passes your test, and at least every 20 minutes.
- A **branch** is an experiment: a copy where you try something risky without touching the version that works. If it is good you **merge** it. If not, you discard it and nothing happened.
- **Rollback** returns the app to any earlier checkpoint, in seconds. The worst case of a bad request becomes "go back twenty minutes".

Rollback has a limit worth knowing before you rely on it. It restores the code. It does not restore what is in the database, emails that were already sent, or what customers already saw. A change that deletes or rewrites data needs its own care: ask the assistant what the change does to existing rows before you approve it.

You ask for all of it in plain language: *save a checkpoint called "login working"*, *start a branch to try a new layout*, *go back to the checkpoint before the PDF export*.

That gives every test in the lab one of two places. **On your laptop**, before the checkpoint: the app runs on your own machine and only you can see it. **At the public address**, after the checkpoint: a phone or a second device can open it, about a minute later. A test on a real phone always belongs to the second kind.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-commits"></div>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="In the business"}
This is how good operations teams already work: change one thing on the line, measure, keep or revert. The history is also your audit trail. When Diego asks why the discount field disappeared last Tuesday, the timeline answers in one click, and when you hand the prototype to engineering in session 4, the record of what was tried and why is worth more to them than the code.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="vc-practice">
<p class="vc-practice-t"><span>Practice · Topic 2</span></p>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">After one request for three features, the quote list stopped loading. You described the bug precisely once and the fix did not work. What is the fastest way forward?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Reading code you cannot evaluate is slow and rarely conclusive for someone who does not program.">Read through the code the assistant wrote for the three features until you spot the line that is wrong.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>Roll back to the last checkpoint and ask for the three features again one at a time, testing after each.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="A second and a third fix on top of three tangled changes usually add a fourth change and a new problem.">Describe the bug again in other words and keep asking for fixes until the list loads as it did before.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">One precise description is worth trying: a bug is a conversation. When that fails on a tangle of changes, going back to the last state that worked and adding the changes one by one isolates the cause in minutes. This is why checkpoints and small steps belong together.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">When should your team save a checkpoint?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Once a day is too rare. A bad change in the afternoon would cost you most of a day.">At the end of each working day, with the date in the name so that the history reads like a calendar.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>After every story that passes your test, with a name that says what works, and at least every 20 minutes.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="A checkpoint is only useful if it captures a state that works. Saving broken states defeats the purpose.">After every single request to the assistant, whether or not the result passed your test, to lose nothing.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">A checkpoint is a state you would be happy to return to. Name it after what works, so rolling back is a choice between meaningful states and not between timestamps.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Diego wants to try a radical redesign of the quote list while Paula's login story is half built. What should he do?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>Start a branch for the redesign, so the working version and the login work stay untouched until it is merged.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="In the same version, the redesign's breakage interrupts the login work and nobody knows which change caused what.">Make the changes directly in the working version, since the assistant can always repair what the redesign breaks.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="A manual copy loses the shared history and turns joining the two versions into hand work.">Copy the whole project to another folder on his laptop and build the redesign there, away from Paula's work.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">A branch is exactly this: an experiment that cannot break the working app. Merge it when it passes the test, or discard it at no cost.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Topic 3 · Where the data lives {#topic-3}

```{=html}
<p class="vc-guide"><strong>Guiding question:</strong> why did the quote requests disappear when Paula refreshed the page?</p>
```

QuoteDesk v0 kept its quote requests in the page: they existed only in the browser that created them, as "today's list on that device". Refresh, and they are gone. Open the app on Diego's phone, and the list is empty. That is normal for a first hour and useless for a second rep.

Data can live in three places. **In the page**: instant, free, gone on refresh. **In a file** on the server: survives refresh, but two reps saving at once can overwrite each other and nothing says who is who. **In a managed database**: a service that stores rows, serves many users at once, keeps backups, and comes with **authentication** (the login: who are you) built in. For anything two people will use, the database is the answer, and the assistant sets it up in a few requests.

The login matters beyond security. It ties each quote request to the rep who created it, and it lets the app have two roles from today: rep and manager, with Carla's account as the manager. In v1 the quote requests are a shared queue that every signed-in rep sees, so that anyone can pick up a waiting customer. Priced quotes, with their discounts, will be private to the rep who owns the customer and to Carla. That second rule is not built by a login; it is the subject of session 4.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-data"></div>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="In the business"}
"Where does the data live?" is the first question legal, IT and finance will ask, long before they ask what the app does. "In a managed database, in a named region, with a login per rep" is the answer that lets a prototype be piloted with real customers. "On my laptop" is the answer that ends the meeting.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="vc-practice">
<p class="vc-practice-t"><span>Practice · Topic 3</span></p>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Paula and Diego save quote requests at the same moment. Which storage choice handles this safely?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Each browser holds its own copy. Neither rep would ever see the other's requests.">In the page, held in each rep's browser memory.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="One file on the server can be overwritten when two people save at once, and it has no idea of users.">In one shared file kept on the server.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>In a managed database with a login per rep.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">A managed database is built for many people writing at once and records who created each row. The other two break as soon as there is a second person.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">QuoteDesk v1 has a login. Marcos signs in. What has the app established?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>Who he is, so what he saves is tied to him. What he may see is a separate rule still to be written.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="That is authorization: what a known user is allowed to see or do. A login alone does not provide it, as session 4 shows.">That he can see only his own customers' priced quotes, because the login filters everything by rep.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Encryption protects data on the way or in storage. It is a different mechanism from identifying the user.">That everything he types is encrypted, so nobody else at Cerro Azul or outside can read his quotes.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">Authentication answers "who are you". Authorization answers "what may you do". QuoteDesk v1 needs the first; assuming it gives you the second is the mistake session 4 opens with.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Topic 4 · UX for output that is sometimes wrong {#topic-4}

```{=html}
<p class="vc-guide"><strong>Guiding question:</strong> Paula will trust QuoteDesk once. What makes her trust it the second time?</p>
```

Next session QuoteDesk will read a pasted message and propose the items: 20 cajas of aceite 900 cc, 5 sacos of arroz, "lo de siempre de lácteos". The last one is a guess. If the app shows that guess with the same confidence as the first two, Paula learns after one wrong delivery that nothing on the screen can be trusted. Then she checks every line, and the app saves nobody any time.

Four patterns fix this. They are decisions you write into the story, not into the code:

- **Show confidence.** Lines the model is unsure about look different and say why.
- **Stream the result.** Items appear as they are produced, so a three-second wait looks like progress and not like a frozen screen.
- **Honest errors.** When there is nothing to extract, the app says "no items found in this message" and offers the manual form, not an empty table.
- **Let the user correct.** Every proposed line can be edited in place and the correction is saved. The app is never the last word.

The model will be wrong some of the time whatever you do. The experience decides whether being wrong costs a glance or costs a customer.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-ux"></div>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="In the business"}
Trust can be measured: how often reps edit a proposed line, how often they give up and retype, how many wrong deliveries trace back to a quote. Once reps use the tool, the correction button gives you that data for free, and the corrections become new examples for the test set you start in session 3.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="vc-practice">
<p class="vc-practice-t"><span>Practice · Topic 4</span></p>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">The model is unsure what "lo de siempre de lácteos" means for Doña Elsa. What should the screen do?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Hiding the uncertainty means Paula finds out from the customer, after the delivery.">Show the best guess as a normal line like the others, so the screen stays clean and quick to scan.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>Show the guess marked as uncertain, with the reason, and make it one tap to confirm or to edit it.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Dropping the line silently loses something the customer asked for. A visible, editable guess is better than a missing line.">Leave the line out of the proposal altogether, so that nothing wrong can ever be shown to the rep.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">Visible uncertainty plus an easy correction is the pattern. Paula spends two seconds on the one line that needs her and trusts the rest.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">A customer writes only "hola, me llamas?". What should QuoteDesk show?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="An empty table looks like a bug, not like a message with no order in it.">An empty items table with the usual columns, ready for the rep to fill in by hand.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="A generic error does not say what happened or what to do next, so the rep goes back to the old way.">A red banner saying that something went wrong and asking the rep to try again later.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>That no items were found, with the manual form and a call-back note one tap away.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">An honest error says what happened and what the user can do next. It keeps Paula inside the tool.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Topic 5 · Teach the assistant how you work: project instructions and skills {#topic-5}

```{=html}
<p class="vc-guide"><strong>Guiding question:</strong> you have explained Cerro Azul's quote format to the assistant four times this week. Where should that explanation live so that you never type it again?</p>
```

### Three things people call "the AI"

Before teaching "the assistant" anything, be exact about which one. From this session on, three different things are in play, and most confusion in AI projects comes from blurring them.

| | What it is | Who uses it | What it can reach |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The building assistant** | The agentic coding assistant your team builds QuoteDesk with | Your team, while building | The repository and its project instructions, plus the assistant's own skills and connectors |
| **A rep's assistant** | The assistant Paula or Carla uses directly for daily work: drafting a quote, summarizing calls, the morning digest | A rep or a manager, every day | The same skills and connectors, with that person's own access. Not the project instructions |
| **The model inside QuoteDesk** | The model that the deployed app calls through an API (an API is the door through which one program asks another for a service) | Nobody directly; the app calls it | Only what the app sends it, and only the tools the app defines. No skills, no connectors |

In this course one assistant app plays both parts: opened on the repository it is the building assistant; opened anywhere else it is your rep's assistant.

The consequence matters for your milestone. Everything in this topic and the next extends the first two, never the deployed app. The project instructions belong to the repository and reach only the building assistant. The skill and the connector you deliver in M2 belong to the assistant itself and work in any conversation. QuoteDesk cannot open a skill or pass through a connector. In session 3 it gets its prices from its own products table, imported from the price sheet.

### Project instructions and skills

The assistant starts every session knowing nothing about Cerro Azul. It does not know that a quote request is not a quote, that a *caja* of aceite holds 12 bottles, or that only Carla approves discounts. So far you have repeated these things in every prompt. There are two better places to put them, and they do different jobs.

**Project instructions** are a plain-text file in the project that the assistant reads at the start of every session. Different tools give it different names (for example `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`); the idea is the same. It holds what is always true: what the product is, your vocabulary, the rules ("one story per change", "all money in CLP without decimals", "ask before touching the login") and how you want changes reported. Because it is always loaded, every line is paid for in every session. Keep it under a page. It lives in the repository, so only the building assistant reads it.

**Skills** hold procedures that are needed only sometimes. A skill is a folder with a file called `SKILL.md`: a name, a one-line description that says when to use it, and the steps. It can carry other files too: a template, examples, even small scripts. The assistant sees only the names and descriptions of your skills until a request matches one, and then it opens that folder and follows it. This is called progressive disclosure, and it is why twenty installed skills cost almost nothing until one is used. The format was published as an open standard in December 2025 and dozens of assistants and coding tools support it, so a skill written for one tool usually works in another. In this course you keep your skill among the assistant's own skills, not inside the QuoteDesk repository, so that it is available in any conversation.

| | Loaded | Good for | At Cerro Azul |
|---|---|---|---|
| A prompt | Once, now | A one-off request | "Summarize yesterday's calls" |
| Project instructions | Every session, always | Rules and vocabulary that never change | "Money in CLP, no decimals. Never change the login without asking." |
| A skill | Only when a request matches its description | A procedure with steps, a template and examples | "How we write a quote", "the Monday sales note" |

One detail decides whether a skill works: **the description is the trigger**. It is the only part the assistant reads before choosing. "Formats quotes" gives it nothing to match. "Drafts or checks a Cerro Azul quote in the house format. Use whenever the user asks for a quote, cotización or price offer for a customer" tells it what the skill does and when to open it. Try both below.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-skills"></div>
```

One caution for later. A skill from the internet is a stranger's instructions, and sometimes a stranger's code, running with your access. Read it yourself before you install it; the assistant may help you read it, but its verdict is not the control. Session 4 treats this as what it is: a supply chain.

::: {.callout-tip title="In the business"}
A skill is how know-how stops living in Paula's head. When Carla changes the discount rule, she edits one file and every assistant that has the skill installed follows the new rule from the next request. That is process documentation that executes itself, and it deserves what any process document gets: an owner, a date, and a review when the process changes.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="vc-practice">
<p class="vc-practice-t"><span>Practice · Topic 5</span></p>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">"All money in CLP without decimals. Never change the login without asking first." Where do these two rules belong?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="A skill is opened only when a request matches its description. These rules must hold in every request, including the ones no skill matches.">In a skill called house-rules, so that they sit with the other procedures of the team.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>In the project instructions file, because they apply to every request in the project.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Repeating rules by hand is what you are trying to stop, and the day you forget is the day the login changes.">At the top of every prompt, typed again each time, so the assistant always sees them.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">What is always true goes in project instructions, which are always loaded. What is needed sometimes, and has steps, goes in a skill.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Your team installed the quote-format skill. Paula asks her assistant for a quote for Doña Elsa and gets a generic letter with an invented 5% discount. What is the most likely cause?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Length is not the problem: the instructions were never opened. The assistant decides from the description alone.">The skill's instructions are too long, so the assistant stopped reading before reaching the template.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>The description does not say when to use the skill, so the assistant never opened the folder.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="A larger model cannot follow instructions it did not load, and no model knows Cerro Azul's format by itself.">The model is too small for this task, so it could not follow a format with that many columns.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">The description is the trigger. If the skill is right and the output ignores it, fix the description first: say what the skill does and when to use it, in the words a rep would use.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Diego finds a "sales-email-writer" skill online with thousands of downloads and wants to install it for the team. What comes first?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>Open the folder and read SKILL.md and any script in it, as you would read a contract before signing.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Popularity is not a review. Malicious skills have been found in public registries, and a skill runs with your team's access.">Install it for the team now: thousands of downloads mean that many people have already checked it.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="The assistant may help you read it, but its verdict is not the control. Read it yourself.">Ask the assistant whether the skill is safe, and install it for the team if the answer is yes.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">A skill is instructions, and sometimes code, that will act with your permissions. It is short enough to read in five minutes. Read it yourself, and prefer writing your own for anything that touches customers.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Topic 6 · Connect the assistant to your systems: connectors and MCP {#topic-6}

```{=html}
<p class="vc-guide"><strong>Guiding question:</strong> the price list lives in Drive and the customers live in the ERP. How does your team's assistant reach them without you copying and pasting?</p>
```

Until now the assistant has known only what you pasted into it. Ask it what aceite 900 cc costs for Minimarket Los Aromos and it has two honest options: say it does not know, or guess. The answer sits in two systems it cannot see.

A **connector** gives the assistant a door into one of those systems. Underneath, most connectors use the same open standard, the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**, introduced in late 2024 and since handed to a neutral foundation, so that a connector built once works with many assistants. Each system is presented by a small program called a server, which offers three things:

| A server offers | Which means | At Cerro Azul |
|---|---|---|
| Tools | Actions the assistant can ask for | "look up a price", "find a customer", "send an email" |
| Resources | Data it can read | the price list, the delivery policy document |
| Prompts | Ready-made requests | "weekly price changes" |

You rarely build one. For Drive, email, calendars, the common CRMs and databases they already exist, and in most assistants you switch them on in a settings screen. Signing in uses the "Sign in with…" window you already know (the standard is called OAuth), and it has a consequence worth saying aloud: the assistant gets **at most the access of the person who signed in**, narrowed by the permissions the connector asks for. If Paula cannot open the payroll folder, neither can her assistant. What Paula can open, her assistant can usually open too. One exception to watch: a connector set up with a shared service account gives everyone who uses it that account's access, whoever they are.

That makes every connector a decision about access. Three rules cover most of it:

1. **Read before write.** A connector that can only read can produce a wrong answer. One that can send or write can produce a wrong action.
2. **One system at a time.** Add a door, use it for a week, then add the next. If five open at once you cannot tell which one caused the problem.
3. **What comes back is data, not instructions.** A document or an email fetched through a connector may contain text that looks like an order. Session 4 shows what happens when the assistant obeys it.

Skills and connectors complement each other. The skill is *how we write a quote*. The connector is *where the prices are*. With both, Paula's one-line request to her assistant produces a quote in the house format with prices read from the list, not guessed. Remember whose doors these are: they belong to the team's assistants. The deployed QuoteDesk does not pass through them.

```{=html}
<div class="vc-widget" data-widget="c2-mcp"></div>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="In the business"}
A manager should be able to say, in one sentence, which systems the assistant can read, which it can change, and who approved that. Start with the price list, read-only: the worst case is a wrong number on Paula's screen, with the source one click away. Email and ERP orders are a different conversation, and they come with approval in session 3 and with permissions in session 4.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="vc-practice">
<p class="vc-practice-t"><span>Practice · Topic 6</span></p>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Paula's assistant now drafts quotes in the right house format, but the prices are invented. What is missing?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="The format is already right, so the skill is being found and followed. A skill describes how; it does not contain today's prices.">A better description on the skill, so that the assistant finds the prices inside the template.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>A connector to the price list, so that the assistant reads the prices and does not guess them.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="No model, of any size, knows Cerro Azul's price list. It needs access, not more capacity.">A larger model, because bigger models have seen more price lists and guess them more accurately.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">The skill is how; the connector is where. Invented prices mean the assistant has the procedure and no access to the data.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Which connector should the team switch on first for its assistants?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Creating orders is the most consequential action available. A mistake there reaches the warehouse and a truck.">ERP orders with write access, because creating the order is where most of the reps' time is saved.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="With five new doors opened together you cannot tell which one caused a problem, and two of them can act on customers.">All five at once, so the team sees in one afternoon everything that the assistant is able to do.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>The price list, read-only: useful today, and the worst case is a wrong answer that Paula can check.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">Read before write, one system at a time. Pick the door with the most value and the smallest worst case, and open the next one after a week of use.</p>
</div>
<div class="vc-quiz">
<p class="vc-quiz-q">Paula connects her assistant to Drive by signing in with her own account. What can the assistant read?</p>
<div class="vc-quiz-opts">
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="Access follows the person who signed in. Folders Paula cannot open stay closed to her assistant.">Everything in Cerro Azul's Drive, because the connector belongs to the company account.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-correct>At most what Paula herself can open, which may be far more than the price list.</button>
<button class="vc-quiz-opt" data-why="The sign-in grants access to her account, not to one file. Unless the connector is limited to a folder, everything she can open is in reach.">Only the price list, because that is the one file she asked the assistant about.</button>
</div>
<p class="vc-quiz-fb">The assistant can reach at most what Paula can open, narrowed by the permissions the connector asks for. If that is too wide, share a single folder with a dedicated account, or limit the connector to that folder.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Critique and reflection

Two teams show one user story end to end: paste a message, pick the customer, save, refresh, sign in as a second rep. The class then asks each presenting team for two things live: roll back one change, and make the quote-format skill trigger without naming it. The rubric criterion in focus this session is **functionality**: does the product work for its user end to end, including the cases that should fail?

Reflection prompt for your build log: *what did the assistant guess that you should have specified, and which line would you now add to your acceptance criteria, your project instructions or your skill?*

## Before next session

Milestone **M2** is due before session 3. It is a team deliverable worth 20%:

- the deployed prototype v1, with sign-in and persistent data;
- three working user stories with their acceptance criteria;
- the link to the private repository, with named checkpoints and one rollback in its history;
- the project instructions file in the repository;
- one skill for your team's assistant (quote-format, or the equivalent for your case), with a screenshot of it triggering;
- one read-only connector for your team's assistant, with a screenshot of its test;
- each member's build log.

Pre-work for session 3: read the Class 3 page (about 100 minutes) and Anthropic's *Building effective agents* (about 20 minutes). Complete the section "Before session 3" of the [setup guide](setup.html) (about 25 minutes): a developer account with the model provider, a monthly spending limit, and one key typed only into your hosting platform. Then collect 20 to 30 messages that your AI feature will receive: real ones with names, phone numbers and addresses changed, or realistic ones you write, each with the items a careful rep would extract from it. This becomes your test set.

## Summary

- The assistant builds what you specify and guesses the rest. Three to six acceptance criteria remove the guesses.
- One story per request. Test by using, not by reading. Ask "what did you change and why?"
- A checkpoint is a state that worked, with a name, sent to GitHub; that is what updates the public address. Test on your laptop before it and at the public address after it. A branch is an experiment that cannot break the working app. Rollback makes small steps cheap, and it restores the code, not the data or the emails already sent.
- Data for two or more people belongs in a managed database with a login. Authentication is "who are you"; authorization comes in session 4.
- Four UX patterns for output that is sometimes wrong: visible confidence, streaming, honest errors, user correction.
- Three things are called "the AI": the building assistant, a rep's assistant, and the model inside QuoteDesk. Project instructions live in the repository and reach only the building assistant. Skills and connectors belong to the assistant and work in any conversation. None of them reaches the deployed app.
- Project instructions hold what is always true and are always loaded, so keep them short. A skill holds a procedure and is opened only when a request matches its description. The description is the trigger.
- A connector is a door into one system, with at most the access of whoever signed in. Read before write, one system at a time, and treat what comes back as data.
